Text says it drew almost ten million visitors, nearly one-fifth of the US population, and it is the core subject of the Philadelphia chapter.

text: Peterson, Asian Self-Representation at World's Fairs (2020)
what_the_text_says: The first large world's fair in the US. Like the Crystal Palace Exhibition it kept the term 'exhibition', reflecting its origins as an outgrowth of trade fairs.

text: Filipová (ed.), Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840-1940 (2015)
what_the_text_says: World exhibition commemorating the centenary of the Declaration of Independence, described as the first of the commemorative fairs. The Spanish contingent travelled to it.

text: Filipová (ed.), Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840-1940 (2015)
what_the_text_says: Philadelphia world's fair celebrating the American centennial. Its successor institution is the Pennsylvania Museum and School of Industrial Art. Finnish participants and attention were drawn to it.

text: Greenhalgh, Ephemeral Vistas (1988)
what_the_text_says: Celebrated a century of American independence and worked out the organisational base for American world's fairs: federal, state and private funding and a Centennial Board of Finance. Traditional fairground stalls and American Indian displays were on site.

text: Greenhalgh, Ephemeral Vistas (1988)
what_the_text_says: Philadelphia centenary of American independence; it had the first Woman's Pavilion, a large art section in Memorial Hall, and British revivalist pavilions by Thomas Harris. The text also covers the US Government Building.

text: Raizman & Robey (eds.), Expanding Nationalisms at World's Fairs (2018)
what_the_text_says: Philadelphia centennial world exhibition. Japan's teahouse, bazaar and residence stood apart on the grounds; Swedish and Norwegian exhibits included wax tableaux; Giuseppe Ferrari's carved presentation cabinet was shown.

text: Raizman & Robey (eds.), Expanding Nationalisms at World's Fairs (2018)
what_the_text_says: The Centennial International Exhibition in Philadelphia, cited in the bibliography (including a study of a carved cabinet by Giuseppe Ferrari shown there) and in the index.

text: Geppert, Fleeting Cities (2010)
what_the_text_says: First exposition to let each participating nation erect its own pavilion, instead of one common building. German participation caused a scandal over its supposed poor-quality goods, reported by Franz Reuleaux.

text: Geppert, Fleeting Cities (2010)
what_the_text_says: Text names it as the origin of the pavilion system, which became the defining element of official international exhibitions.

text: Geppert, Fleeting Cities (2010)
what_the_text_says: American Centennial Exhibition at Philadelphia; India participated in it. An 1877 lecture on American industry at this exhibition is cited.

text: Geppert, Fleeting Cities (2010)
what_the_text_says: Centennial International Exhibition at Philadelphia, discussed in Reuleaux's Briefe aus Philadelphia (1877), in studies of German goods (Bonnell 2001; Krutisch on German applied arts 1876) and in the index.

text: Hollengreen et al. (eds.), Meet Me at the Fair (2014)
what_the_text_says: Philadelphia international exhibition commemorating the centennial of the American Revolution. Machinery Hall housed the Corliss steam engine; a Chinese exhibit was unfinished on opening day; the Philadelphia Zoo was designed alongside it. Also cited as the 'International Exhibition, 1876' essay on the chair maker (lines 188, 332).

text: Hollengreen et al. (eds.), Meet Me at the Fair (2014)
what_the_text_says: The Philadelphia International Exhibition of 1876 (Centennial). Text says it ran 159 days; its admissions system (coin tally, turnstile gates, official embossed photo-tickets) is discussed in detail, and it opened with every major building ready. The ticket emboss gives 10 November as the close, the body text 11 November; both are stated.

text: Lawn (ed.), Modelling the Future (2009)
what_the_text_says: Produced 21 railroad cars of exhibits used to found the US National Museum, unveiled Sholes's typewriter, and drew a Japanese government participation focused on craft objects. Germany took part with little success and no own exhibition; Spain's commissioner Lopez Fabra and the education reports (Buisson) are also tied to it.

text: Benedict, The Anthropology of World's Fairs (1983)
what_the_text_says: Had seven main departments, including Education and Science, a Women's Pavilion built with money raised by women, and a Corliss engine that was itself a major attraction. Its amusement section, Shantyville, lay just outside the grounds.

text: Badger, The Great American Fair (1979)
what_the_text_says: The first world's fair on a grand scale held in the United States, celebrating the centennial of American independence; it set records for attendance, fairground area, receipts and the size of a single exhibition building. The Corliss engine was its chief attraction. Appendix A: 236 acres, 30,000 exhibits, attendance 8,004,274; US appropriation $2,183,184.59.

text: Maloney, World's Fair Gardens (2012)
what_the_text_says: The first major United States world's fair after the Civil War, in Fairmount Park; featured a freestanding Horticultural Hall, sunken gardens, carpet bedding, Japanese exhibits and the Corliss engine in Machinery Hall. Designed by H. J. Schwarzmann.

text: Della Coletta, World's Fairs Italian-Style (2006)
what_the_text_says: Commemorated the centenary of American independence, held in Fairmount Park. Its Italian name is taken from a Sonzogno illustrated volume titled L'esposizione universale di Filadelfia del 1876, named in the notes.

text: Molella & Knowles (eds.), World's Fairs in the Cold War (2019)
what_the_text_says: Centennial exposition in Philadelphia; text cites it as the first place women erected a woman's building at an exposition.

text: Molella & Knowles (eds.), World's Fairs in the Cold War (2019)
what_the_text_says: Index entry only (p. 138) in the extract. Full text says a women's building was first erected at this fair (full text line 5546).

text: Boone, 'The Spanish Element in Our Nationality' (2019)
what_the_text_says: Philadelphia centennial world's fair in Fairmount Park. Spain sent an agricultural and industrial display, financed three buildings and lent paintings from its national museum; its history paintings, including Gisbert's Landing of the Puritans, were admired by few US critics. Visitors were more drawn to Cuban cigars, Galician pickled fish and Jerez sherry than to the art, and the Spanish government's own response to the fair was unenthusiastic.

text: Hoffenberg, An Empire on Display (2001)
what_the_text_says: Australian colonies' displays were used to attract settlers; South Australia's label drew more visitor response than Victoria's or Queensland's. Appendix C gives 40,462 pounds of British government expenditure.

text: Hoffenberg, An Empire on Display (2001)
what_the_text_says: Victoria, New South Wales and the British section sent exhibits; Victorian commissioners reported in 1877 and an article on Australia at the exhibition is cited.

text: Çelik, Displaying the Orient (1992)
what_the_text_says: Frank Furness designed the Brazilian section in the main building in a neo-Islamic style. Cited as a key case for Islamic influence on Western architecture through Owen Jones and Furness.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: Held in Fairmount Park to commemorate the American Declaration of Independence; the first American world's fair with a Memorial Hall for fine arts. Its 13,000 identical bronze medals meant no hierarchical awards, and it lost $1.9 million.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: The 1876 US centennial world's fair, cited as a model that encouraged later fairs; the telephone and phonograph debuted there.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: Centennial exposition in Fairmount Park, the model against which the 1926 Sesqui-Centennial was measured.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: Named only as the '1876 Centennial', from which the text traces American world's fair design to the 1915 Panama-Pacific fair. The city is not stated in the text and is recognised from general knowledge.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: Philadelphia 1876 exposition; the officials index names John Welsh (president of finance) and Joseph R. Hawley (president of the Centennial commission).

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: Centennial Exhibition of 1876. The list cites histories, silver albumen photographs and railroad links to it.

text: Rydell, Findling & Pelle, Fair America (2000)
what_the_text_says: First major American world's fair, authorised by Congress in 1871 and held in Fairmount Park. It was meant to celebrate the centennial and, the text says, helped revive American business confidence after the Panic of 1873 and the cultural success of its exhibits; its popularity led to the 1884-85 New Orleans fair.

text: Harvey, Hybrids of Modernity (1996)
what_the_text_says: Named in the text only as 'Philadelphia in 1876' in an Official Guide quote, where Bell's telephone, Edison's telegraph, early sewing machines and typewriters were presented. Fair name from general knowledge.

text: Roche, Mega-Events and Modernity (2000)
what_the_text_says: US centenary expo presented as a celebration of a century of national progress. Bell's telephone was first demonstrated to a mass public here, and a Women's Building was housed in it. The text also records the Plains Indians' defeat of US forces during the expo. Table 2.1 records a loss.

text: Mandell, Paris 1900 (1967)
what_the_text_says: Large international exhibition, listed among the post-1851 fairs. The text notes the telephone was shown there; it is not described further.

text: Allwood, Allan & Reid, The Great Exhibitions: 150 Years (2001)
what_the_text_says: Celebrated the centenary of the USA in Fairmount Park (236 acres for the main area), with individual pavilions, a Women's Pavilion and Alexander Graham Bell's telephone. Opened 10 May 1876 with Wagner's Centennial Inauguration March. The Main Building was torn down in 1880.

text: Allwood, Allan & Reid, The Great Exhibitions: 150 Years (2001)
what_the_text_says: US centennial exposition; the text notes that Congress made a federal loan so construction could be completed. Table: loss $5.166m (£1.065m); 284.5 acres; open 5.3 months.

text: Giberti, Designing the Centennial (2002)
what_the_text_says: Authorised by Congress in March 1871 to celebrate the centennial of American independence; held in Fairmount Park under the U.S. Centennial Commission, with a dual national and typological classification and a single large Main Building. The text also notes that Campbell first proposed a Centennial exhibition in an 1864 Smithsonian speech.

text: Giberti, Designing the Centennial (2002)
what_the_text_says: The US Centennial International Exhibition. Text describes its six-month run and its classified installation, and draws a parallel with the Wanamaker store. Only passing mentions in this extract; the 1876 passages were left out.

text: Karp & Lavine (eds.), Exhibiting Cultures (1991)
what_the_text_says: Text notes that a few live Native Americans appeared there, before ethnographic villages became central at the 1889 Paris fair. Hazelius's wax tableaux were also shown at this world's fair.

text: Ganz, The 1933 Chicago World's Fair (2008)
what_the_text_says: Philadelphia's centennial exhibition. It included a women's building and a female board of managers but gave women no official committee status, a limit that later American fairs continued.

text: Samuel, The End of the Innocence (2007)
what_the_text_says: Philadelphia world's fair where Susan B. Anthony and other suffragettes presented a 'Declaration of the Rights of Women' to acting vice president Thomas W. Ferry.

text: Samuel, The End of the Innocence (2007)
what_the_text_says: Alexander Graham Bell gave the first public demonstration of his telephone there. The text says it was believed to have helped unite the country after the Civil War.

text: Hotta-Lister, The Japan-British Exhibition of 1910 (1999)
what_the_text_says: Japan shipped more than 7,000 packages, a number exceeded only by Britain. The text links it to growing American knowledge of Japan. Expenditure 359,545 yen (appendix).

text: Burris, Exhibiting Religion (2001)
what_the_text_says: First major international exposition in the United States, which set the tone for Chicago 1893; its displays of Native American cultures were meant to be educational.

text: Hur, Staging Modern Statehood (dissertation)
what_the_text_says: Official invitation delivered to China; the Chinese exhibit was assembled through the Maritime Customs. Japan took a more active approach to it than to earlier fairs.

text: Gelernter, 1939: The Lost World of the Fair (1995)
what_the_text_says: Gelernter's list of earlier world's fairs includes the American Centennial exhibit at Philadelphia in 1876. Mentioned only in passing.

text: Weimann, The Fair Women (1981)
what_the_text_says: The first American fair of real international importance after London 1851. Elizabeth Gillespie led the women's fundraising, and the women's space was promised in the Main Building.

text: Shepherdson-Scott, Exhibiting (Japanese) Manchuria at Chicago (article)
what_the_text_says: Japan's first exhibit in America, focused on products made for US tastes; it helped open export markets for Japanese goods.

text: Brown, Fair Japan (article)
what_the_text_says: The first American world's fair. A Japanese-style garden was built there, the first 'Japanese garden' in North America, and the Japanese brought kudzu vine.

text: Kaiser, The Great Derby Race (article)
what_the_text_says: The first American world exhibition, which made a strong impression on Europeans and commemorated US independence. The Corliss engine was its greatest attraction.

text: Gilbert, Perfect Cities (1991)
what_the_text_says: Its Corliss steam engine was bought by George Pullman and installed in his company town.

text: Maxwell, Colonial Photography and Exhibitions (1999)
what_the_text_says: Intended to show America's machines and wealth; the first American exhibition of world-class standard. Barnum ran Shantyville on the Midway with 'Fijian Man-eaters'; a women's department was included, and African-Americans were prevented from mounting displays. Herbert Deveril's New Zealand Maori photographs were made for it.

text: Filipová (ed.), Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840-1940 (2015)
what_the_text_says: First Finnish industrial and art exhibition, which opened in July 1876, a quarter century after the Crystal Palace. It drew the national spotlight while the world looked to Philadelphia.

what_the_text_says: Listed only in Appendix D ('Fairs Not Included'), which says it fell short of the book's inclusion criteria; no other detail is given.

what_the_text_says: South African colonial exhibition in the British Empire series described by MacKenzie.

text: Allwood, Allan & Reid, The Great Exhibitions: 150 Years (2001)
what_the_text_says: First South African International Exhibition; the start of the exhibition wave in the British Empire.

what_the_text_says: Early regional exhibition in northern Bohemia to revive regional production and trade.

what_the_text_says: Specialised Madrid exhibition of wine-making products, machines, apparatus and tools for vinification.

what_the_text_says: Appendix A lists it as Sydney Industrial and Intercolonial (1877). A visitor found its many objects scarcely possible to inspect.

text: Hoffenberg, An Empire on Display (2001)
what_the_text_says: Report of the Canadian Commissioner at the Exhibition of Industry held at Sydney in 1877.

text: Giberti, Designing the Centennial (2002)
what_the_text_says: A permanent show run by the International Exhibition Company in the Centennial's Main Building, opened May 10 1877 with President Hayes; it dropped competitive awards and used a thirty-category classification. It failed financially, reopened in May 1879, and in January 1881 its directors recommended closing it; the building was sold and demolished.

text: Giberti, Designing the Centennial (2002)
name_in_text: Permanent International Exhibition (International Exhibition Company, Philadelphia)
what_the_text_says: The 'new Exhibition of 1877' opened after the Centennial, run by the International Exhibition Company in the Centennial buildings in Fairmount Park. Start date is the opening-ceremony date cited in the notes. Notes cite New York Times pieces on its end in 1879 and again in 1881. Text treats it as an exhibition with commercial and museum-like aspects.

text: Hur, Staging Modern Statehood (dissertation)
name_in_text: First Domestic Encouragement of Industry Exhibition
what_the_text_says: The first of Japan's Domestic Encouragement of Industry Exhibitions, held after the Meiji government's experience at Vienna (1873) and Philadelphia (1876). The text calls it the 'sprout' of a future World Exhibition in Japan; the 1903 Osaka exhibition was three times its size.

text: Hur, Staging Modern Statehood (dissertation)
name_in_text: First Domestic Encouragement of Industry Exhibition
what_the_text_says: The first of Japan's Domestic Encouragement of Industry Exhibitions, on a site of about 25 acres, cited as a benchmark for the scale of the Nanyang Industrial Exposition (which had about 165 acres). The text does not give the year; 1877 is from general knowledge and should be checked.

text: Filipová (ed.), Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840-1940 (2015)
what_the_text_says: The first of the government's national domestic expositions, held at Ueno Park in Tokyo while the Satsuma Rebellion was being fought. The text says it drew 500,000 visitors in three months, after which the state decided to hold one every four years.

text: Lawn (ed.), Modelling the Future (2009)
what_the_text_says: Japan's first domestic exhibition, which opened three days after the Educational Museum. It followed the Philadelphia classification except that 'Education and Knowledge' became 'Fine Arts', with educational apparatus placed under 'Produce'. The Ueno Park venue is from the Osaka text and general knowledge.

text: Filipová (ed.), Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840-1940 (2015)
what_the_text_says: First of Japan's national industrial expositions, held at Ueno Park in Tokyo. Its success led the state to decree one every four years.

text: Lawn (ed.), Modelling the Future (2009)
what_the_text_says: Japan's first national domestic industrial exhibition, held by the government in the style and classification of the international fairs. Design sketches prepared by the Exhibition Bureau for craft wares were reused here and at the 1876 and 1878 fairs. The city is not named in the extract; Tokyo is inferred.

text: Hotta-Lister, The Japan-British Exhibition of 1910 (1999)
what_the_text_says: The first of the government's national industrial expositions, held in a purpose-built building in Ueno Park. Exhibits were grouped by category, and the show spawned Kankojo shops selling unsold exhibits.

text: Hur, Staging Modern Statehood (dissertation)
name_in_text: First Domestic Encouragement of Industry Exhibition
what_the_text_says: First of the five national Domestic Encouragement of Industry Exhibitions (Naikoku Kangyō Hakurankai) staged by the Meiji state; the text presents the series as central to Meiji exhibition policy.

what_the_text_says: Tunisian palace-style structures were featured at the 1878, 1889 and 1900 Paris expositions (Hanson). Hedrick notes that the 1878 'Avenue of Nations' extended the national-pavilion format introduced in 1867.

text: Hur, Staging Modern Statehood (dissertation)
what_the_text_says: The Chinese exhibit was arranged through the IMCS and drew criticism; Marquis Zeng Jize called it lacking core products and questioned entrusting it to Westerners. Guo Songtao visited the fair, and Chinese high officials came to the site without being commissioners.

text: Lawn (ed.), Modelling the Future (2009)
what_the_text_says: Japanese educational exhibits won admiration, and the Educational Museum is credited with helping. Teaching materials were bought in London for it and design sketches from the Exhibition Bureau were used.

text: Peterson, Asian Self-Representation at World's Fairs (2020)
what_the_text_says: One of a succession of increasingly massive Paris expositions (with 1889 and 1900) which the text cites as the origin of the French usage of 'exposition'. No further detail in the extract.

text: Filipová (ed.), Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840-1940 (2015)
what_the_text_says: Exposition Universelle with a joint Austro-Hungarian representation; known for the Rue des Nations exotic villages, a captive look-out balloon and a Machine Gallery whose plan was reused in Barcelona 1888.

text: Filipová (ed.), Cultures of International Exhibitions 1840-1940 (2015)
what_the_text_says: Universal exposition in Paris at which the Rue des nations displayed national styles. Finland's commissioner was Robert Runeberg, and Finnish companies repeated displays first shown in Helsinki.

text: Greenhalgh, Ephemeral Vistas (1988)
what_the_text_says: Third Paris exposition, held in the mood of recovery after the Commune; a financial disaster whose losses changed the funding system for later Paris shows. It housed the Palais du Trocadéro and the first Rue de Caire.

text: Greenhalgh, Ephemeral Vistas (1988)
what_the_text_says: Exposition Universelle with the Palais du Trocadero and an Exposition Historique; its fine art selection excluded many avant-garde artists, marking a rift between the Beaux-Arts and the avant-garde (text cites Zola).

text: Raizman & Robey (eds.), Expanding Nationalisms at World's Fairs (2018)
what_the_text_says: Paris universal exposition. Its Avenue of Nations anticipated the national-pavilion arrangement; Italian decorative-arts displays of luxury furniture were criticised; Sweden and Norway offered life-size mannequin interiors. Tunisian structures were shown at the 1878, 1889 and 1900 Paris expositions.

text: Raizman & Robey (eds.), Expanding Nationalisms at World's Fairs (2018)
what_the_text_says: Universal exposition in Paris, known here from an international jury report on furniture and decorative arts (Group III, classes 17-18) and from the index (Prussian section).

text: Geppert, Fleeting Cities (2010)
what_the_text_says: Third Parisian universal exposition, with the Palais du Trocadéro. Germany did not take part, a decision the text links to the 1876 Philadelphia scandal. Its native-village (village indigène) annex is one of the first of its kind.

text: Geppert, Fleeting Cities (2010)
what_the_text_says: About 53,000 exhibitors; Germany did not take part. Text gives 571,792 persons visiting Paris during the exposition, a city figure rather than fair admissions.

text: Geppert, Fleeting Cities (2010)
what_the_text_says: Paris universal exhibition; the text discusses the reasons for Germany's non-participation in it.

text: Geppert, Fleeting Cities (2010)

text: Hollengreen et al. (eds.), Meet Me at the Fair (2014)
what_the_text_says: Known in this volume only from an essay title (Lawrence Bird, on dreaming of work at the fair).

text: Hollengreen et al. (eds.), Meet Me at the Fair (2014)
what_the_text_says: Paris World Exhibition of 1878, held in the Palais du Champ de Mars; the chapter reads its main building and its machine gallery through engravings and the official illustrated publications.

text: Lawn (ed.), Modelling the Future (2009)
what_the_text_says: Japan's educational exhibits were admired; Spain's Instituto Cardenal Cisneros won a gold medal; Germany stayed away for political reasons. The Manier map of national education caused a dispute with Spain, and the Musee Pedagogique was founded in 1879 in the context of this fair.

text: Benedict, The Anthropology of World's Fairs (1983)
what_the_text_says: Spread across both sides of the Seine and symbolised by the twin-towered Palais du Trocadero, with French exhibitors in one half and foreign ones along a rue des nations. It hosted 32 international congresses.

text: Badger, The Great American Fair (1979)
what_the_text_says: Presented as proof that the Third Republic was established and could accomplish as much as Napoleon III's empire had done. Appendix A: 66 acres, 52,835 exhibits, attendance 16,032,725; US appropriation $190,000.

text: Rydell, World of Fairs (1993)
what_the_text_says: Named in Leon Blum's epigraph on Universal Expositions and political crises. The city is inferred from the Paris sequence in the same passage, not stated in the extract.

text: Della Coletta, World's Fairs Italian-Style (2006)
what_the_text_says: Trocadero towers and the prototype of the Rue des Nations, where participating nations expressed their individuality within a shared civilizing progress.

text: Boone, 'The Spanish Element in Our Nationality' (2019)
what_the_text_says: Cited only in passing: a critic said Spanish painting at the 1889 Paris exhibition was still the same kind of work Spain had shown at the 1878 world's fair. The text does not name the city; Paris is inferred from general knowledge.

text: Hoffenberg, An Empire on Display (2001)
what_the_text_says: Colonial and British Indian courts were prominent; 206 selected Indian artisans were funded to visit and report on their trades. A journalist complained about the ticket-photograph problem at the gates. Royal Commission expenditure was 73,712 pounds per Appendix C.

text: Hoffenberg, An Empire on Display (2001)
what_the_text_says: British Indian Section handbook and South Australian commission papers document Indian and colonial participation.

text: Çelik, Displaying the Orient (1992)
what_the_text_says: Known for the Trocadero Palace (Davioud and Bourdais), which kept the 1878 outline in its successor. Egyptian section with Mariette-Bey's retrospective of antiquities. Tunisian and Moroccan displays and a Persian palace (Palace of Mirrors). Rue des Nations street of nations. The text states the Ottoman Empire did not take part.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: The Third Republic's showpiece exposition, on the Champ de Mars extended to Trocadero; it had 52,835 exhibitors and 29,810 awards, and 32 congresses. The official opening was 1 May 1878, though the text says the real opening is sometimes given as 20 May.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: Paris world's fair whose Palais du Trocadero was later demolished for the 1937 fair; a reproduction Cairo street first appeared there and was reused in 1889.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: Named as the source of the Trocadero Palace, which was leveled in 1934 (the text calls the palace the principal legacy from the 1878 exposition universelle). No dates or figures are given.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: Paris exhibition of 1878 (Jean Baptiste Krantz, commissioner general); the text notes that one library holds more than 50 books and pamphlets on the Paris 1878 exposition alone.

text: Findling & Pelle (eds.), Encyclopedia of World's Fairs and Expositions (2008)
what_the_text_says: Paris world's fair of 1878.

text: Roche, Mega-Events and Modernity (2000)
what_the_text_says: Third Paris Exposition Universelle in the 1855-1900 series, with national pavilions and the start of imperial sections presented as exotic cities of pavilions. De Coubertin attended as a teenager. Table 2.1 records a loss.
